newsitem.title: USA: Brazil's Malan downplays concerns about trade gap.
newsitem.headline: Brazil's Malan downplays concerns about trade gap.

text.p: Brazilian Finance Minister Pedro Malan on Monday played down concerns over his country's bulging trade deficit and rejected suggestions that currency devaluation was the best way to correct it.
In a speech to the International Monetary Fund's policy-making Interim Committee, Malan argued that the Brazilian currenct account deficit was not very high by international standards.

The deficit is currently running at about the equivalent of 3.6 percent of Brazilian gross domestic product. Malan said that much of it -- 40 percent -- is being financed by foreign direct investment.

"The proper macroeconomic response to a current account deficit which is seen as high or as rising is not, in our case at least, either reliance on devaluation or protectionism, but an increase in domestic savings," he said.
The best way to accomplish that is through a reduction in Brazil's public sector deficit, via privatization, pension reform and other measures, Malan said.
The Brazilian finance minister also reiterated his determination to contain inflation. "We are not going to give up our fight to keep inflation under control," he said.
Malan was generally upbeat about the outlook for the world economy. However, he cautioned that there were some risks.
"Higher interest rates in the United States may cause turbulence in the international financial markets, affecting capital flows," he said.
"A longer delay in economic recovery in continental Europe may hamper the exports of developing countries," he added.
